name: Masada
focus: Earth, timber, and a natural spur.
description: Watch a supply line build an earthen approach over the western spur. When the surface is ready, a timber tower can climb toward the casemate wall.
fact: The western ramp, siege camps, and encircling wall survive. The ramp was built on a natural spur; the Romans did not build the mountain. The siege is commonly dated to 73 or 74 CE.
limit: The plateau, camps, and ramp are schematic. Construction speed, worker numbers, tower motion, and the breach sequence are illustrative. Details of the final assault and the historical narrative remain debated.
sources: Roman ramp, Israel Nature and Parks Authority

name: Alesia
description: Builders extend two defensive circuits around the hilltop settlement. Roman patrols hold the space between them while a relief force approaches from outside.
fact: Caesar enclosed the oppidum with an inner line and protected his troops with an outer line. Archaeological investigations have recovered the defensive lines, camps, and military material.
limit: The two circuits are compressed into a small landscape. The model simplifies the valleys, ditch systems, troop numbers, and attacks. It does not reconstruct a particular hour of the battle.

name: Jerusalem
description: Work crews build approach terraces beneath the northern defenses. Towers and artillery support an assault against several walls around a dense urban model.
fact: Roman forces under Titus besieged Jerusalem in 70 CE. Josephus describes siege banks, engines, successive walls, and assaults during the siege.
limit: This is a schematic engineering vignette, not a surveyed reconstruction of Jerusalem or a complete account of the siege. Buildings, banks, and positions are simplified; the destruction of civilians is not simulated.

name: Tyre
focus: Make a road across the sea.
description: Haulers carry rubble from the shore and extend a causeway toward an island city. Ships circle the works and towers advance as the stone surface emerges from the water.
fact: Alexander’s forces besieged the island city in 332 BCE. A causeway linked it to the mainland, permanently changing the coastline.
limit: The island, channel, causeway, fleet, and construction rate are stylized. Ships follow simple steering paths; the water surface is a wave model. This is not a sediment transport or naval warfare reconstruction.
sources: Tyre archaeological research, American University of Beirut

name: Constantinople
description: Crews prepare protected gun positions and bring ammunition forward. Heavy cannon fire physical projectiles toward a miniature section of the layered land walls.
fact: The Ottoman siege of 1453 overcame Constantinople’s defenses. The surviving land walls are part of the Historic Areas of Istanbul World Heritage property.
limit: This model shows a selected landward sector. The coastline and buildings are schematic; cannon behavior, wall damage, units, and construction rates are illustrative. It does not model the full campaign.

name: Candia
focus: An approach to a bastioned city.
description: Digging crews push zigzag trenches toward the Venetian bastions. Supply carriers move between the camp and batteries while cannon exchange fire over the earthworks.
fact: Candia, present-day Heraklion, was a Venetian city besieged by Ottoman forces from 1648 to 1669. Contemporary maps show the fortified city and siege operations.
limit: The star-shaped walls and trench system are schematic, not a tracing of a historical map. This compressed scenario does not reproduce twenty-one years of fighting or the underground mining campaign.
sources: Contemporary siege map, Royal Collection Trust
